categories.label: Technical Architecture of Blockchain-Enabled Smart Contracts
categories.memo: Covers the technological components and implementation architecture needed to operationalize smart contracts for construction contract administration, including data inputs, oracles, and platform choices.

codes.label: Blockchain Platform and Data Verification Infrastructure
codes.description: Use of blockchain platforms (e.g., Ethereum), IPFS, and related infrastructure to store immutable records and trigger contract execution.

sub_codes.label: Manual vs Automated Input Verification
sub_codes.description: Current implementations often still rely on manual verification/entry of data by a general contractor or central database, limiting full decentralization.

codes.label: IoT and Real-Time Monitoring Integration
codes.description: Integration of IoT sensors, RFID, and monitoring thresholds to detect real-world events (e.g., structural thresholds, delivery arrivals) that trigger smart contract execution.

codes.label: Image/Oracle-Based Documentation for Dispute Reduction
codes.description: Use of blockchain oracles and objective image-based documentation to verify performance and reduce disputes over progress and payment conditions.

codes.label: Smart Contract Code vs Smart Legal Contract Distinction
codes.description: Differentiating the technical code implementation of a smart contract from its legal enforceability status, relevant to adoption and governance.

categories.label: Automated Payment and Cash Flow Management
categories.memo: Addresses how blockchain smart contracts automate progress payments, billing, and cash flow processes specifically in fragmented MMC/prefabrication supply chains.

codes.label: Automated Progress Payment Frameworks
codes.description: Staged frameworks (preparation, initialization, execution) that encode billing plans and trigger fund transfers automatically upon verified task completion, reducing reliance on third parties.

codes.label: Cash Flow Barriers in Modular/Offsite Construction
codes.description: Financial barriers such as high initial capital costs and payment delays that are exacerbated by fragmented MiC supply chains, motivating blockchain-based solutions.

codes.label: Procurement System and Cash Flow Interdependency
codes.description: Recognition that procurement/delivery approaches shape cash flow dynamics differently in OSC/MiC projects than in conventional construction, an underexplored contractual relationship.

codes.label: Partial Automation Limitations of Existing Payment Systems
codes.description: Existing BIM-blockchain payment systems require manual data updates and do not account for disputes or multiple delivery systems, indicating incomplete automation.

categories.label: Incentive and Penalty Allocation Mechanisms
categories.memo: Focuses on methods for deriving fair, quantitative rules for reward/penalty allocation among project participants, especially using cooperative game theory and simulation.

codes.label: Shapley Value-Based Reward/Penalty Allocation
codes.description: Use of the Shapley value algorithm to fairly allocate rewards or penalties among fabricators, crane operators, workers, and subcontractors based on marginal contribution to project outcomes.

codes.label: Simulation-Derived Incentive Rules
codes.description: Discrete-event or scenario simulation used to generate data-driven incentive/penalty thresholds and strategies (e.g., delivery variability thresholds, workforce reassignment) for embedding into smart contracts.

codes.label: Real-Time vs End-of-Project Penalty Enforcement
codes.description: Contrast between traditional practice of enforcing delay penalties only at/near project completion and smart contracts' capacity for real-time, continuous incentive enforcement.

codes.label: Objective Quantified Performance Appraisal
codes.description: Replacing subjective, qualitative subcontractor performance appraisal with objective, quantified performance-based incentive/penalty structures.

categories.label: Constraint and Coordination Management via Smart Contracts
categories.memo: Deals with how smart contracts encode and manage production and coordination constraints specific to prefabrication/MMC workflows (fabrication, logistics, installation).

codes.label: Make-Ready and Constraint Removal Automation
codes.description: Smart contracts encoding rules for timely identification and removal of production constraints (e.g., material arrival, crane availability, labor) before task release.

codes.label: Prefabrication Supply Chain Coordination Constraints
codes.description: Coordination challenges among fabricator batch production preferences, crane/logistics scheduling, and on-site installation labor that smart contracts must account for.

codes.label: External Environmental Impact on Bottlenecks
codes.description: Weather and other external conditions shifting production bottlenecks between off-site fabrication and on-site installation, affecting contractual constraint modeling.

codes.label: Decentralized vs Centralized Coordination Authority
codes.description: Tension between smart contracts' potential to decentralize construction management decisions and the continued reliance on centralized project managers/authority.

categories.label: Limitations and Governance Gaps of Smart Contracts
categories.memo: Captures the recognized shortcomings of smart contracts as automated contractual instruments, including irreversibility, inflexibility, and governance/regulatory gaps that current frameworks (including CCDC) would need to address.

codes.label: Irreversibility and Immutability Risks
codes.description: Smart contract executions are irreversible once triggered, requiring exhaustive pre-specification of scenarios and creating risk of financial loss from poorly designed rules or errors.

codes.label: Inflexibility for Change Orders and Unexpected Events
codes.description: Smart contracts function as attachments to conventional contracts and lack flexibility to handle change orders, unforeseen ('black swan') events, or complex multiparty scenarios.

codes.label: Governance Model and Dispute Resolution Gaps
codes.description: Absence of a mature governance model specifying rights, obligations, and sanctions for noncompliance, and lack of mechanisms for post-deployment adjustment or dispute resolution.

codes.label: Regulatory, Interoperability, and Cost Barriers to Adoption
codes.description: Broader institutional barriers to smart contract adoption including regulatory uncertainty, technical interoperability, and initial investment costs.

codes.label: Human Oversight Requirement
codes.description: Continued necessity of human oversight and verification (e.g., by qualified technicians) to prevent errors such as false positives despite automation.

codes.label: Persistent Bureaucratic/Administrative Delays
codes.description: Smart contracts shorten but do not eliminate bureaucratic and administrative phases such as funding approvals and permitting.

categories.label: Lifecycle Extension and Application Scope
categories.memo: Addresses the expansion of smart contract applications beyond design/construction payment automation into maintenance, emergency response, and decommissioning phases of infrastructure.

codes.label: Emergency Response Automation
codes.description: Smart contracts triggering automated actions (alerts, data logging, infrastructure closure) when IoT-monitored thresholds are exceeded, reducing legal disputes and delays.

codes.label: Maintenance and Decommissioning Phase Integration
codes.description: Extension of smart contract application beyond construction into asset maintenance and decommissioning, an area traditionally underexplored relative to payment automation during design/construction.

codes.label: Financial Safeguards via Pre-Allocated Funds
codes.description: Use of pre-allocated funds and verification mechanisms within smart contracts to ensure payments occur only after qualified approval, safeguarding financial operations across lifecycle phases.

categories.label: Relational and Contractual Alternatives to Centralized Control
categories.memo: Explores how smart contracts interact with or challenge existing relational contracting models (e.g., IPD) and centralized risk allocation practices in construction.

codes.label: Relational Contracting (IPD) Risk/Reward Sharing
codes.description: Integrated Project Delivery and similar relational models attempt to align subcontractor interests via shared risk/reward, though fair allocation remains challenging, motivating smart-contract-based alternatives.

codes.label: Contractual Insufficiency of Coercive Hierarchical Control
codes.description: Recognition that hierarchical authority and standard contractual terms alone cannot guarantee reliable collaboration or prevent opportunistic subcontractor behavior.

codes.label: Single Point of Failure in Centralized Data Reliance
codes.description: Reliance on a trustful central database for smart contract inputs creates risk of failure, pointing to need for decentralized verification mechanisms in future contract systems.
